svg.title: Two ceilings on one prompt: the window that fills, and the accuracy that slides first
svg.desc: A single horizontal bar represents the context window for one pass. Reading left to right, it is divided into three parts: a fixed block for the system prompt and tool definitions, a much wider block for the transcript which grows on every pass, and a reserved block of headroom at the right for the tool result and the model's own output on this pass. A solid line at the far right edge marks the hard ceiling, where the window is full and the request fails outright. Below the bar, a dashed line slopes downward from left to right to represent measured accuracy, and it is already falling well to the left of the right edge. A highlighted vertical marker sits in the middle of the bar, labelled to show that accuracy is already degrading there, long before the window is full. A footer states that the slope shape is illustrative only, because the measured curves are non-uniform and differ by model, and that there is no onset point: the decline runs the whole length of the bar and the marker is one place on it rather than where it begins.
svg.text: ONE PASS · WHAT THE MODEL IS HANDED

svg.text: CEILING 2 — attention. No error, no log line.
This one binds first, and it is the one you get asked about.
The slope is schematic, not a measurement: Chroma found degradation is real across all 18 models it tested, but non-uniform and different for each one.
There is no onset point. The slide runs the length of the bar, and the marker is one place on it — not where it begins.
